claim: The BioMe biobank comprises over 38,000 participants.
source: With over 38000 participants, the BioMe biobank, at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York City (NYC), is one of the most diverse cohorts ascertained at a single urban medical center under a uniform study protocol.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of participants in the BioMe biobank.

claim: Over 65% of BioMe participants self-report as Black/African-American or Hispanic/Latino/a.
source: The BioMe biobank comprises a highly diverse cohort, with over 65% of participants self-reporting as Black/African-American or Hispanic/Latino/a, and over 35% born outside mainland US, representing more than 110 countries of origin.
evidence: The manuscript provides demographic statistics from the BioMe biobank.

claim: Over 35% of BioMe participants were born outside mainland US.
source: The BioMe biobank comprises a highly diverse cohort, with over 65% of participants self-reporting as Black/African-American or Hispanic/Latino/a, and over 35% born outside mainland US, representing more than 110 countries of origin.
evidence: The manuscript provides demographic statistics from the BioMe biobank.

claim: BioMe participants represent more than 110 countries of origin.
source: The BioMe biobank comprises a highly diverse cohort, with over 65% of participants self-reporting as Black/African-American or Hispanic/Latino/a, and over 35% born outside mainland US, representing more than 110 countries of origin.
evidence: The manuscript provides demographic statistics from the BioMe biobank.

claim: 701 individuals in BioMe had primary or secondary relationships with another participant.
source: We observed that 701 individuals had primary (parent-child, sibling) or secondary (avuncular, grandparental) relationship with another participant in BioMe, and we removed these individuals from all downstream analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of related individuals detected using RELATEAdmix.

claim: Elevated levels of distant relatedness were observed in Ashkenazi Jewish populations in BioMe.
source: We observed elevated levels of distant relatedness in both the AJ (median summed length of IBD sharing within population = 44.7 cM; 95% C.I. = 44.66–44.82 cM) and HL (16.2 cM; 16.18–16.22 cM) populations, compared to AA (3.77 cM; 3.76–3.77 cM) or non-AJ EA (4.5 cM; 4.45–4.55 cM) populations (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports median IBD sharing statistics and references Figure 1A showing the distribution.

claim: Elevated levels of distant relatedness were observed in Hispanic/Latino/a populations in BioMe.
source: We observed elevated levels of distant relatedness in both the AJ (median summed length of IBD sharing within population = 44.7 cM; 95% C.I. = 44.66–44.82 cM) and HL (16.2 cM; 16.18–16.22 cM) populations, compared to AA (3.77 cM; 3.76–3.77 cM) or non-AJ EA (4.5 cM; 4.45–4.55 cM) populations (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports median IBD sharing statistics and references Figure 1A showing the distribution.

claim: Elevated distant relatedness in Ashkenazi Jewish populations is congruent with previous reports of founder effects.
source: This is congruent with previous reports of founder effects in both AJ populations (Need et al., 2009) and in some H/L populations (Moreno-Estrada et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies reporting founder effects in these populations.

claim: Elevated distant relatedness in Hispanic/Latino/a populations is congruent with previous reports of founder effects.
source: This is congruent with previous reports of founder effects in both AJ populations (Need et al., 2009) and in some H/L populations (Moreno-Estrada et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies reporting founder effects in these populations.

claim: The founder effect in Hispanic/Latino/a populations was predominantly driven by the Puerto Rican-born group.
source: We examined IBD tract length distributions within H/L sub-continental populations and observed that the founder effect was predominantly driven in the Puerto Rican-born group (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of IBD tract length distributions and references Figure 1C.

claim: 2816 Hispanic/Latino/a individuals in the BioMe discovery cohort were estimated to be of Puerto Rican ancestry.
source: In total, we estimated 2816 H/L in the BioMe discovery cohort were of Puerto Rican ancestry, and focused the downstream analysis on this group as the largest founder population in BioMe.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of individuals classified as Puerto Rican ancestry.

claim: Height is highly heritable and polygenic.
source: Height is known to be highly heritable and polygenic (Visscher et al., 2010; Lango Allen et al., 2010), however, extremes of short stature can be caused by rare variants in single genes with large effect sizes (Durand and Rappold, 2013a).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the heritability and polygenic nature of height.

claim: Extremes of short stature can be caused by rare variants in single genes with large effect sizes.
source: Height is known to be highly heritable and polygenic (Visscher et al., 2010; Lango Allen et al., 2010), however, extremes of short stature can be caused by rare variants in single genes with large effect sizes (Durand and Rappold, 2013a).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on genetic causes of short stature.

claim: 56 Puerto Ricans in BioMe met the clinical definition of short stature.
source: We noted that 56 Puerto Ricans met the clinical definition of short stature (Cohen et al., 2008) (range of short stature 5'1'−4'0' in men, and 4'8'−3'8' in women) defined as 2 standard deviations below the population-specific mean for men and women separately (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of individuals meeting clinical criteria for short stature.

claim: One IBD-clique at locus 9q32 achieved genome-wide significant association with height under a recessive model.
source: Adjusting for 480 tests (Bonferroni adjusted threshold p<1×10−4) one IBD-clique achieved a genome-wide significant signal at the locus 9q32 (IBD-clique frequency = 0.012; β = −3.78; p<2.57×10−11) (Figure 2A), spanning a large mapping interval chr9:112 MB-120MB.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical association results from IBD mapping analysis.

claim: The significant IBD-clique at 9q32 contains 59 individuals, 56 heterozygous and 3 homozygous.
source: The clique contains 59 individuals, 56 of whom are heterozygous and 3 are homozygous for the associated IBD haplotype.
evidence: The manuscript reports the composition of the significant IBD-clique.

claim: The three homozygous individuals were 6-10 inches shorter than the population mean for height in the Puerto Rican cohort.
source: The three individuals driving the recessive signal, two women and one man, were less than 2.5 s.d. shorter (height reduction range 6'−10') than the population mean for height in the Puerto Rican cohort (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the height measurements of homozygous individuals.

claim: The minimum shared boundary of the significant IBD-haplotype overlapped the gene COL27A1.
source: The IBD-haplotypes driving the signal spanned a genic region with several candidate loci, and the minimum shared boundary overlapped a single gene, COL27A1, which encodes for Collagen Type XXVII, Alpha 1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the genomic location of the IBD haplotype and references Figure 2C.

claim: Whole genome sequencing revealed a missense mutation in COL27A1 (p.G697R, rs140950220) in all four homozygous individuals.
source: Examination of variants that were observed in at least 6 copies between the four individuals (to account for sequencing error or missing calls) revealed a single candidate coding allele, a missense mutation in Collagen Type XXVII, Alpha 1 (COL27A1, g.9:116958257.C>G, NM_032888.1, p.G697R, rs140950220) (Supplemental file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of whole genome sequencing analysis.

claim: The COL27A1 p.G697R variant is predicted to be damaging by in silico analysis.
source: In silico analysis suggest that this glycine residue is highly conserved, and that a molecular alteration to arginine at this position is predicted to be damaging (SIFT score = 0.0; PhyloP score = 2.673; GERP NR score = 5.67).
evidence: The manuscript reports in silico prediction scores for the variant.

claim: The COL27A1 p.G697R variant was previously implicated as causal for Steel syndrome in a Puerto Rican family.
source: These findings are consistent with a recent report implicating the same COL27A1 variant as causal for the rare orthopedic condition Steel syndrome in a Puerto Rican family (Gonzaga-Jauregui et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study linking the variant to Steel syndrome.

claim: Steel syndrome was first described in 1993.
source: First described in 1993, the main clinical features of Steel syndrome include short stature, bilateral hip and radial head dislocations, carpal coalition (fusion of the carpal bones), scoliosis, pes cavus (high arches), and dysmorphic features (Steel et al., 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites the original description of Steel syndrome.

claim: The main clinical features of Steel syndrome include short stature, bilateral hip and radial head dislocations, carpal coalition, scoliosis, pes cavus, and dysmorphic features.
source: First described in 1993, the main clinical features of Steel syndrome include short stature, bilateral hip and radial head dislocations, carpal coalition (fusion of the carpal bones), scoliosis, pes cavus (high arches), and dysmorphic features (Steel et al., 1993).
evidence: The manuscript cites the original description of Steel syndrome clinical features.

claim: There was 100% concordance between the COL27A1 p.G697R variant and the significant IBD-haplotype in homozygotes.
source: This demonstrated 100% concordance between the COL27A1.pG697R variant and the significant IBD-haplotype in homozygotes (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports genotyping validation results.

claim: Two Puerto Rican participants in the phase 3 1000 Genomes Project reference panel were carriers of the COL27A1 p.G697R variant.
source: We note that two Puerto Rican participants in the phase 3 1KGP reference panel were carriers of the COL27A1.pG697R variant, raising the possibility that we may have been able to detect this association using more a traditional SNP association approach.
evidence: The manuscript reports the presence of the variant in the 1000 Genomes Project data.

claim: The IBD haplotype had better concordance with true COL27A1 p.G697R homozygous state (100%) compared to 1000 Genomes Project imputation (66.67%).
source: Upon examination of the correlation between the imputed COL27A1.pG697R and the true carrier status of homozygotes, we noted a concordance of only 66.67%, indicating that the IBD haplotype was a better tag of the true COL27A1.pG697R homozygous state compared to 1KGP imputation in the Puerto Rican cohort (Supplemental file 3).
evidence: The manuscript compares concordance between IBD mapping and imputation approaches.

claim: The association between COL27A1 p.G697R and clinical short stature was replicated in 1775 Puerto Rican individuals from the PAGE Study.
source: The association between COL27A1.pG697R and clinical short stature was replicated using a cohort of 1775 individuals of self-reported Puerto Rican ancestry from BioMe that were not included in the discovery analysis, that were genotyped on the Illumina Infinium Multi-Ethnic Genotype Array (MEGA) as part of the Polygeneic Architecture using Genomics and Epidemiology (PAGE) Study.
evidence: The manuscript reports replication analysis in an independent cohort.

claim: The replication analysis showed strong association of COL27A1 p.G697R with height under a recessive model (β = −3.5; p<4.87×10−07).
source: The COL27A1.pG697R (rs140950220) variant was directly genotyped on MEGA, and an association of the variant under a recessive model resulted in a strong signal of association (allele frequency = 0.017; β = −3.5; s.e. = 0.70; p<4.87×10−07).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical association results from the replication analysis.

claim: The replication analysis revealed 51 additional BioMe carriers and two homozygous individuals for COL27A1 p.G697R.
source: The replication analysis revealed 51 additional BioMe carriers and two individuals that were homozygous for the variant.
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of carriers identified in the replication cohort.

claim: Both homozygous participants in the replication cohort were short statured (2.4 and 3.6 s.d. from the sex specific population mean).
source: The two homozygous participants were both short statured (2.4 and 3.6 s.d from the sex specific population mean).
evidence: The manuscript reports the height measurements of homozygous individuals in the replication cohort.

claim: None of the five homozygous patients had a clinical diagnosis of Steel syndrome in their electronic health records.
source: Of note, there was no evidence that any of the five patients had a clinical diagnosis of Steel syndrome.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from manual review of electronic health records.

claim: All five homozygous individuals had EHR-documented evidence of several Steel syndrome characteristics.
source: In all five individuals, however, we found EHR-documented evidence of several previously described Steel syndrome characteristics, including developmental dysplasia of the hip (or congenital hip dysplasia), carpal coalition, scoliosis, and cervical spine anomalies (Table 1) (Steel et al., 1993; Flynn et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from manual review of electronic health records and references Table 1.

claim: The incidence of cervical spine anomalies in homozygous patients (4 out of 5) was higher than previously reported.
source: The incidence of cervical spine anomalies, including cord compression and spine surgeries, was higher than previously reported (four out of five patients).
evidence: The manuscript compares observed incidence to previous reports.

claim: COL27A1 is a fibrillar collagen that contributes to the structural integrity of the extracellular matrix.
source: COL27A1 is a fibrillar collagen, which are a class of collagens that contribute to the structural integrity of the extracellular matrix (Pace et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on the function of COL27A1.

claim: Enrichment of COL27A1 RNA expression in vertebrae, long bones, eyes, and lungs has been observed in embryonic mice.
source: Enrichment of COL27A1 RNA expression in vertebrae, as well as long bones, eyes, and lungs has previously been observed in embryonic mice (Pace et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on COL27A1 expression patterns.

claim: A mouse deletion of 87 amino acids of the COL27A1 homolog exhibited severe chondroplasia consistent with clinical features observed in homozygotes.
source: A mouse deletion of 87 amino acids of the COL27A1 homolog exhibited severe chondroplasia consistent with clinical features observed in homozygotes (Plumb et al., 2011), a similar musculoskeletal phenotype was observed in knockdown of the col27a1a and col27a1b genes in zebrafish (Christiansen et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on COL27A1 function in animal models.

claim: Knockdown of col27a1a and col27a1b genes in zebrafish resulted in a musculoskeletal phenotype similar to that observed in mice.
source: A mouse deletion of 87 amino acids of the COL27A1 homolog exhibited severe chondroplasia consistent with clinical features observed in homozygotes (Plumb et al., 2011), a similar musculoskeletal phenotype was observed in knockdown of the col27a1a and col27a1b genes in zebrafish (Christiansen et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on COL27A1 function in animal models.

claim: Type alpha-1 collagen genes contain a conserved Gly-Xaa-Yaa repeat in their triple helical domain.
source: Type alpha-1 collagen genes, of which COL27A1 is a member, contain a conserved Gly-Xaa-Yaa repeat in their triple helical domain (Persikov et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on collagen structure.

claim: Substitution of glycine for arginine in the COL27A1 triple helix would likely destabilize helix formation through steric hindrance.
source: We observed that the glycine residues occupied the center of the crowded triple helix, and that substitution for a bulkier arginine would likely destabilize helix formation through steric hindrance (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports structural modeling results and references Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Many other collagen disorders are driven by molecular alterations of a glycine in the triple helix of the underlying collagen genes.
source: We note that many other collagen disorders, including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (McGrory et al., 1996; Tromp et al., 1995; Anderson et al., 1997), Alport syndrome (Knebelmann et al., 1992; Zhou et al., 1992) and Osteogenesis Imperfecta (Starman et al., 1989; Shapiro et al., 1992), are driven by molecular alterations of a glycine in the triple helix of the underlying collagen genes.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on other collagen disorders.

claim: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Alport syndrome, and Osteogenesis Imperfecta are inherited under an autosomal dominant mode.
source: However, all of these disorders are inherited under an autosomal dominant mode, in contrast to Steel syndrome, which has only been reported as a recessive disease.
evidence: The manuscript states the inheritance pattern of these disorders based on established knowledge.

claim: Steel syndrome has only been reported as a recessive disease.
source: However, all of these disorders are inherited under an autosomal dominant mode, in contrast to Steel syndrome, which has only been reported as a recessive disease.
evidence: The manuscript states the reported inheritance pattern of Steel syndrome.

claim: Five ICD9 codes achieved significant association (FDR < 0.05) with COL27A1 p.G697R carrier status in PheWAS analysis.
source: Of the five significantly associated ICD9 codes (False Discovery Rate (FDR) < 0.05), three involved the musculoskeletal system 730.08 (pGLM < 7.1 × 10−6; odds ratio (OR) = 34.5; 95% Confidence Interval (CI) = 7.4–162), 721.0 (pGLM < 6.6 × 10−5; OR = 5.4; CI = 2.4–12.3), and 716.98 (pGLM < 4.4 × 10−4; OR = 5.8; CI = 2.2–15.3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical association results from PheWAS analysis.

claim: Three of the five significantly associated ICD9 codes involved the musculoskeletal system.
source: Of the five significantly associated ICD9 codes (False Discovery Rate (FDR) < 0.05), three involved the musculoskeletal system 730.08 (pGLM < 7.1 × 10−6; odds ratio (OR) = 34.5; 95% Confidence Interval (CI) = 7.4–162), 721.0 (pGLM < 6.6 × 10−5; OR = 5.4; CI = 2.4–12.3), and 716.98 (pGLM < 4.4 × 10−4; OR = 5.8; CI = 2.2–15.3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical association results from PheWAS analysis.

source: Of the five significantly associated ICD9 codes (False Discovery Rate (FDR) < 0.05), three involved the musculoskeletal system 730.08 (pGLM < 7.1 × 10−6; odds ratio (OR) = 34.5; 95% Confidence Interval (CI) = 7.4–162), 721.0 (pGLM < 6.6 × 10−5; OR = 5.4; CI = 2.4–12.3), and 716.98 (pGLM < 4.4 × 10−4; OR = 5.8; CI = 2.2–15.3).

claim: Manual review of chart records revealed that ICD9 code 730.08 referred to vertebral osteomyelitis in the three carriers with this code.
source: Manual review of chart records for these patients revealed that this code referred to vertebral osteomyelitis in the three carriers with the ICD9 code.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from manual chart review.

claim: ICD9 code 721.0 (cervical spondylosis without myelopathy) was significantly associated with COL27A1 p.G697R carrier status (p < 6.6 × 10−5; OR = 5.4).

source: Of the five significantly associated ICD9 codes (False Discovery Rate (FDR) < 0.05), three involved the musculoskeletal system 730.08 (pGLM < 7.1 × 10−6; odds ratio (OR) = 34.5; 95% Confidence Interval (CI) = 7.4–162), 721.0 (pGLM < 6.6 × 10−5; OR = 5.4; CI = 2.4–12.3), and 716.98 (pGLM < 4.4 × 10−4; OR = 5.8; CI = 2.2–15.3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical association results from PheWAS analysis.

claim: Manual review of chart records revealed that ICD9 code 716.98 referred to knee arthropathy in all four patients with this code.
source: Manual review of chart records for these patients revealed that this code referred to knee arthropathy in all four patients.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from manual chart review.

claim: Manual chart review found an increased risk of cervical stenosis in 15% (5/34) of carriers compared to 0% (0/31) of controls (p<0.05).
source: Specifically, we found an increased risk of cervical stenosis in 15% (5/34) of carriers compared to 0% (0/31) of controls (p<0.05).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from manual chart review with statistical comparison.

claim: Manual chart review showed a trend of 2-fold higher rates of scoliosis (24%; p<0.35) in carriers compared to non-carriers.
source: Although not reaching statistically significance, we show a trend of 2-fold higher rates of scoliosis (24%; p<0.35), arthritis (38%; p<0.1), and lumbar spine degradation (29%; p<0.25) in carriers compared to non-carriers and previous published reports in similar age groups (Kebaish et al., 2011; Reginster, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from manual chart review with statistical comparison.

claim: Manual chart review showed a trend of 2-fold higher rates of arthritis (38%; p<0.1) in carriers compared to non-carriers.
source: Although not reaching statistically significance, we show a trend of 2-fold higher rates of scoliosis (24%; p<0.35), arthritis (38%; p<0.1), and lumbar spine degradation (29%; p<0.25) in carriers compared to non-carriers and previous published reports in similar age groups (Kebaish et al., 2011; Reginster, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from manual chart review with statistical comparison.

claim: Manual chart review showed a trend of 2-fold higher rates of lumbar spine degradation (29%; p<0.25) in carriers compared to non-carriers.
source: Although not reaching statistically significance, we show a trend of 2-fold higher rates of scoliosis (24%; p<0.35), arthritis (38%; p<0.1), and lumbar spine degradation (29%; p<0.25) in carriers compared to non-carriers and previous published reports in similar age groups (Kebaish et al., 2011; Reginster, 2002).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from manual chart review with statistical comparison.

claim: 38% (13/34) of carriers showed evidence of spine degeneration compared to 13% (4/31) of non-carriers (p<0.03).
source: In general, 38% (13/34) of carriers showed evidence of spine degeneration varied from severe (multiple level cord compression and neurological symptoms necessitating corrective surgery) to moderate (lower back pain with no neurological symptoms managed with physical therapy and/or pain medication) compared to 13% (4/31) of non-carriers (Fishers exact test p<0.03).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from manual chart review with statistical comparison.

claim: The carrier rate of COL27A1 p.G697R is estimated to be 1:51 in Puerto Rican-born individuals (MAF = 1.1%).
source: We estimate the carrier rate of COL27A1.G697R to be 1:51 in Puerto Rican-born individuals (minor allele frequency (MAF) = 1.1%); 1:9 in individuals born on the island of St. Thomas (MAF = 11%); 1:346 in Hispanic/Latino/as in the US (MAF = 0.29%) and 1:72 in BioMe Hispanic/Latino/a populations from New York City (MAF = 0.7%); and 1:746 in individuals born in the Dominican Republic (MAF = 0.067%) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports carrier frequency estimates from global screening and references Figure 4A.

claim: The carrier rate of COL27A1 p.G697R is estimated to be 1:9 in individuals born on the island of St. Thomas (MAF = 11%).
source: We estimate the carrier rate of COL27A1.G697R to be 1:51 in Puerto Rican-born individuals (minor allele frequency (MAF) = 1.1%); 1:9 in individuals born on the island of St. Thomas (MAF = 11%); 1:346 in Hispanic/Latino/as in the US (MAF = 0.29%) and 1:72 in BioMe Hispanic/Latino/a populations from New York City (MAF = 0.7%); and 1:746 in individuals born in the Dominican Republic (MAF = 0.067%) (Figure 4A).

evidence: The manuscript reports carrier frequency estimates from global screening and references Figure 4A.

source: We estimate the carrier rate of COL27A1.G697R to be 1:51 in Puerto Rican-born individuals (minor allele frequency (MAF) = 1.1%); 1:9 in individuals born on the island of St. Thomas (MAF = 11%); 1:346 in Hispanic/Latino/as in the US (MAF = 0.29%) and 1:72 in BioMe Hispanic/Latino/a populations from New York City (MAF = 0.7%); and 1:746 in individuals born in the Dominican Republic (MAF = 0.067%) (Figure 4A).

claim: The COL27A1 p.G697R variant is present in only 4 copies in the 60,706 exomes in the ExAC database.
source: Finally, the variant is present in only 4 copies in the 60,706 exomes in the ExAC database (Exome Aggregation Consortium et al., 2016), likely due to differences in the populations comprising both datasets.
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of the variant in the ExAC database.

claim: Local ancestry inference revealed all three homozygous individuals were homozygous for Native American ancestry at the IBD haplotype.
source: Examination of local ancestry on the background of the IBD haplotype in all three homozygous individuals revealed all to be homozygous for Native American ancestry, suggesting the COL27A1.pG697R arose on a Native American haplotype (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports local ancestry inference results and references Figure 4B.

claim: The COL27A1 p.G697R variant arose on a Native American haplotype.
source: Examination of local ancestry on the background of the IBD haplotype in all three homozygous individuals revealed all to be homozygous for Native American ancestry, suggesting the COL27A1.pG697R arose on a Native American haplotype (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript infers the ancestral origin of the variant based on local ancestry analysis.

claim: IBDNe analysis suggested evidence of a strong bottleneck in Puerto Ricans approximately 9–14 generations ago.
source: The analysis suggested evidence of a strong bottleneck in Puerto Ricans approximately 9–14 generations ago, with the smallest effective population sized dating approximately 12 generations ago (estimated Ne = 2580, 95% C.I 2320–2910).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from IBDNe analysis of effective population size.

claim: The smallest effective population size in Puerto Ricans was approximately 12 generations ago (estimated Ne = 2580, 95% C.I 2320–2910).
source: The analysis suggested evidence of a strong bottleneck in Puerto Ricans approximately 9–14 generations ago, with the smallest effective population sized dating approximately 12 generations ago (estimated Ne = 2580, 95% C.I 2320–2910).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from IBDNe analysis of effective population size.

claim: The timing of the bottleneck is consistent with European immigration and slave trading on the Island, resulting in admixture and population bottlenecking.
source: This is consistent with the timing of European immigration and slave trading on the Island, resulting in admixture and population bottlenecking, followed by demographic growth post-contact (Moreno-Estrada et al., 2013; Gravel et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on Puerto Rican demographic history.

claim: There was no evidence of selection at the COL27A1 locus based on integrated haplotype score (iHS) analysis.
source: Finally, to see if there was evidence that the locus had undergone a recent selective sweep we calculated the integrated haplotype score (iHS) (Voight et al., 2006; Szpiech and Hernandez, 2014) across chromosome 9 in phased genotype data for BioMe Puerto Rican samples, but did not observe evidence of selection at the locus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from iHS analysis and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The COL27A1 p.G697R variant arose in the ancestral Native American populations that peopled the Caribbean.
source: Together, this evidence suggests that the COL27A1.pG697R variant arose in the ancestral Native American populations that peopled the Caribbean, which underwent a strong bottleneck during the period of colonization, which may help explain the prevalence of this disease in amongst contemporary Puerto Rican populations.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple lines of evidence to infer the origin of the variant.

claim: The ancestral Native American populations that peopled the Caribbean underwent a strong bottleneck during the period of colonization.
source: Together, this evidence suggests that the COL27A1.pG697R variant arose in the ancestral Native American populations that peopled the Caribbean, which underwent a strong bottleneck during the period of colonization, which may help explain the prevalence of this disease in amongst contemporary Puerto Rican populations.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes multiple lines of evidence to infer demographic history.

claim: The bottleneck during colonization may help explain the prevalence of COL27A1 p.G697R in contemporary Puerto Rican populations.
source: Together, this evidence suggests that the COL27A1.pG697R variant arose in the ancestral Native American populations that peopled the Caribbean, which underwent a strong bottleneck during the period of colonization, which may help explain the prevalence of this disease in amongst contemporary Puerto Rican populations.
